headline: A New Body Scanner Backed by a Spotify Billionaire Comes to the U.S.

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A company called Neko Health has made a special machine that checks your body for health problems. It looks at your skin, blood, and other parts of your body to see if anything is wrong. The company was started in Sweden by two people, one of whom helped create Spotify, the music app. Now Neko Health has come to New York City in the United States. So many people want to try the scan that over 300,000 people have put their name on a waiting list! The scan costs $500 and takes about one hour. Right now, health insurance does not pay for it, so people have to pay for it themselves. The people who made this company hope it can help people find health problems early, before they become serious. Finding problems early can help doctors fix them faster and keep people healthier. The company is now trying to grow in America, but it still needs to follow rules and get permission from the government before it can open in more places.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: A health startup called Neko Health has become very popular, and now it has expanded from Sweden to New York City. The company was created by David Ek, who also helped start Spotify, along with his partner Hjalmar Nilsonne. Neko Health uses advanced technology, including cameras and computer programs, to scan a person's body and check things like their skin, blood, and metabolism, which is how the body turns food into energy. The company has already raised almost $1 billion from investors and has more than 300,000 people waiting to try the scan. Each scan costs $500 and takes about an hour, but health insurance does not pay for it yet. However, people can use special savings accounts made for medical costs. An investor named Farooq Abbasi, who has tried the scan twice, believes it could change how people take care of their health in the future. He says that in the U.S., many people avoid preventative care, which means check-ups that catch health problems early, because it's too expensive. Abbasi hopes Neko Health can make this kind of care cheaper and easier to get. He also says the technology has improved a lot, now testing 55 different health markers instead of just 15. Even though Neko Health is exciting investors and customers, it still needs to grow carefully and follow American health rules before it can open in more cities.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Neko Health, a startup from Sweden, has recently expanded into the United States, opening a location in New York City. The company was founded by David Ek, a cofounder of Spotify, and his business partner Hjalmar Nilsonne. Their idea is to use advanced technology, including computer vision (a type of artificial intelligence that can analyze images), to scan a person's body for early signs of health problems involving the skin, blood, and metabolism. So far, Neko Health has raised almost $1 billion in funding and has a waitlist of more than 300,000 people hoping to try it. Each scan costs $500 and takes about an hour. Since health insurance doesn't currently cover the cost, people must either pay out of pocket or use a Health Savings Account, a special account that lets people save pretax money for medical expenses. Farooq Abbasi, an investor at Preface Ventures who has personally used the scan twice, believes Neko Health could help fix a major problem in American healthcare: many people skip preventative check-ups because they're too expensive or hard to access. He argues that catching health issues early could save lives and money in the long run. Abbasi also points out how quickly the technology has advanced — early versions of the scan tested only 15 biomarkers (measurable signs of health, like cholesterol levels), while the newest version tests 55. He sees this as a sign that artificial intelligence is starting to meaningfully improve medical screening, not just offer another trendy wellness product. Still, Neko Health faces big challenges as it tries to expand across the U.S. It needs government approval to operate more clinics and must prove its technology is both accurate and safe. The American healthcare system is also complicated, with strict regulations and high costs that can make it difficult for new medical companies to grow quickly. Despite these hurdles, Abbasi remains optimistic, believing that with enough investment and support, companies like Neko Health could eventually make preventative healthcare more affordable and available to everyone, not just those who can pay $500 out of pocket.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Neko Health, a Swedish startup cofounded by Spotify's David Ek and his business partner Hjalmar Nilsonne, has officially launched in the United States with a new location in New York City. The company offers a one-hour full-body scan that uses advanced sensors and computer vision—a form of artificial intelligence that analyzes images—to screen for early warning signs in a person's skin, blood, and metabolism. Since its founding, Neko Health has raised nearly $1 billion in funding and built a global waitlist of over 300,000 people eager to try the technology. Despite this popularity, each scan costs $500 and is not currently covered by health insurance, though customers can use Health Savings Accounts, tax-advantaged accounts designed for medical expenses, to help pay for it. Farooq Abbasi, an investor at Preface Ventures who has been scanned twice himself, sees Neko Health as a potential solution to a deep-rooted problem in American healthcare: low participation in preventative care. Preventative care refers to medical checkups and screenings meant to catch health issues before they become serious or expensive to treat. Abbasi argues that cost is a major barrier keeping many Americans from getting these kinds of checkups, and he believes affordable, accessible options like Neko Health could change that. He also highlights how much the company's technology has advanced since he first tried it—early scans measured only 15 biomarkers (specific indicators of health, like blood sugar or cholesterol levels), while the newest scans measure 55. For Abbasi, this progress reflects a broader trend of artificial intelligence transforming healthcare, moving beyond trendy wellness products toward tools that provide real, actionable medical insights. However, Neko Health's path to widespread use in the U.S. isn't guaranteed. The American healthcare system is heavily regulated, and medical technology companies must go through rigorous approval processes to ensure their tools are safe and effective before they can expand to more cities or be covered by insurance. Scaling a physical, hands-on service like a body scanning clinic is also far more complicated and expensive than scaling a digital app, since it requires trained staff, physical equipment, and real estate in every new city. Even so, Abbasi remains hopeful, arguing that continued investment in companies tackling healthcare's biggest problems could eventually make high-quality preventative care both more affordable and more widely available across the country, potentially reshaping how everyday Americans approach their own health.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Neko Health, a Swedish startup cofounded by Spotify's David Ek and entrepreneur Hjalmar Nilsonne, has expanded into the United States with a new clinic in New York City, marking a significant step for a company that has quickly become one of the most talked-about ventures in preventative health technology. The company offers a one-hour, full-body scan that uses advanced sensors and computer vision—a branch of artificial intelligence capable of analyzing visual and physiological data—to detect early indicators of problems involving the skin, blood, and metabolic function. Neko Health has raised nearly $1 billion in funding and amassed a global waitlist exceeding 300,000 people, signaling strong consumer demand despite the service's $500 price tag, which is not currently covered by traditional health insurance. Customers can, however, apply funds from Health Savings Accounts—tax-advantaged accounts specifically designated for medical expenses—toward the cost. Farooq Abbasi, a partner at Preface Ventures and an investor in Neko Health, frames the company's expansion as a potential answer to a long-standing inefficiency in American healthcare: chronically low rates of preventative care utilization. Preventative screenings are widely understood to reduce long-term healthcare costs and improve outcomes by catching conditions early, yet high costs and limited access often discourage people from seeking them out. Abbasi, who has undergone the scan twice, points to the rapid evolution of Neko's technology as evidence of its growing sophistication—early versions of the scan measured just 15 biomarkers, quantifiable indicators of physiological health such as cholesterol or glucose levels, while the current version analyzes 55. He positions this growth within a broader narrative about artificial intelligence's expanding role in medicine, arguing that tools like Neko Health represent a meaningful shift beyond superficial wellness trends toward systems that generate genuinely useful, actionable health data for patients. Still, Neko Health's ambitions face substantial structural obstacles in the U.S. market. Unlike software-based startups that can scale rapidly and cheaply, Neko's business model depends on physical clinics, trained personnel, and specialized equipment, all of which require significant capital and time to establish in each new city. Moreover, the American healthcare system is governed by a dense web of regulatory requirements designed to ensure patient safety and data accuracy, meaning Neko Health must navigate lengthy approval processes before it can expand further or seek insurance coverage. These regulatory and logistical hurdles raise real questions about whether a venture capital-funded startup, however well-capitalized, can sustainably scale a capital-intensive healthcare service nationwide. Despite these uncertainties, Abbasi remains optimistic, suggesting that sustained investment directed toward companies addressing healthcare's core inefficiencies could gradually make high-quality preventative care more accessible and affordable. Whether Neko Health ultimately succeeds in reshaping preventative medicine in America—or remains a costly, exclusive offering for those who can already afford $500 scans—will likely depend on how effectively it balances technological innovation with the practical and regulatory realities of the U.S. healthcare system.

questions: If a health scan like this became common at your school or local clinic, do you think it would be fair that only people who can pay $500 get access to it? Why or why not?
How might catching health problems early, before they get serious, change the way people think about going to the doctor?
Do you think artificial intelligence should play a bigger role in healthcare, like helping to find diseases early? What are some risks or benefits you can think of?
